output.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation demonstrates a posterior cortical profile. Visuospatial and visuoconstructive abilities are markedly impaired: Judgment of Line Orientation 14/30, VOSP Dot Counting 5/10, Rey Complex Figure Copy 18/36 (delayed recall 8/36, limited by the copy). Trail Making A 68 s and B 142 s are slowed, with visual search demands contributing. Verbal episodic memory is within normal limits (CVLT-II long delay free recall 10/16), confrontation naming is preserved (Boston Naming Test 52/60), and letter and category fluency are normal. Geriatric Depression Scale 8/30 (normal range). Screening: MMSE 25/30, MoCA 23/30. Profile is most consistent with a posterior cortical syndrome with visuospatial predominance, at a level consistent with mild dementia given the reported functional decline.

alternatives: Rivastigmine (oral or transdermal) is not metabolised by CYP450 enzymes and avoids the fluoxetine interaction
Galantamine is partly metabolised by CYP2D6 and is affected by fluoxetine in the same way
interactions: Donepezil + Fluoxetine 20 mg: fluoxetine is a strong CYP2D6 inhibitor and can raise donepezil exposure; start at 5 mg, titrate slowly and monitor for nausea, diarrhoea, bradycardia and syncope
Donepezil + Lisinopril: no clinically relevant interaction
Donepezil + Acetaminophen or vitamin D3: no interaction
output.proposed: Donepezil 5 mg once daily at bedtime
warnings: Vagotonic effect: bradycardia, heart block and syncope can occur; baseline heart rate 72 bpm; check pulse at initiation and after each dose increase
Cholinomimetics carry a labelled warning that they may cause generalized convulsions; in a patient with epilepsy, maintain the antiseizure regimen and report any breakthrough seizure
Nausea, diarrhoea and anorexia are common during titration

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MoCA 23/30 with visuospatial and visuoconstructive loss, simultanagnosia and optic ataxia; recall helped by cues; husband confirms 18 months of decline; instrumental independence lost (driving taken over, stopped work): mild dementia
action_criteria.label: Perform a structured cognitive and behavioural assessment with informant history: a validated bedside instrument with the per-domain breakdown, whether delayed recall improves with cueing, and an explicit account of which instrumental activities have been lost. The syndrome must be documented before it is attributed
action_criteria.rationale: Visuospatial complaints in a patient with epilepsy, depression and cataracts have to be measured as a cortical syndrome and staged by function before they are attributed [PCA_consensus_2017].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Marked visuospatial and visuoperceptual impairment (Judgment of Line Orientation 14/30, VOSP dot counting 5/10, Rey copy 18/36) with normal verbal memory, naming and fluency: a posterior cortical syndrome
action_criteria.label: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize the cognitive profile and establish a baseline for tracking
action_criteria.rationale: Normed testing shows a visuospatial-predominant profile with preserved memory, the defining profile of posterior cortical atrophy [PCA_consensus_2017].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TSH, B12, folate, homocysteine, RPR, HIV, renal, hepatic and inflammatory markers normal; levetiracetam level within range: no reversible or medication-level cause
action_criteria.label: Order the cognitive laboratory panel to identify reversible or contributing causes
action_criteria.rationale: Treatable contributors must be excluded before a neurodegenerative cause is accepted [AAN_dementia_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral parieto-occipital cortical atrophy (right more than left) with relative sparing of medial temporal structures; Fazekas grade 2; no mass or restricted diffusion
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI with dementia (volumetric) protocol to define the atrophy pattern and exclude stroke, mass, epileptogenic lesion and vascular disease
action_criteria.rationale: MRI excludes a structural or epileptogenic lesion and shows the posterior atrophy that supports a neurodegenerative cause [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amyloid positivity: decreased CSF Abeta42/40 ratio with raised p-tau181 and total tau, or a positive florbetapir PET (SUVr 1.42)
action_criteria.label: Establish amyloid status with CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET when the result would change management
action_criteria.rationale: Either CSF Abeta42/40 with p-tau or amyloid PET establishes amyloid status; one conclusive test is enough, and it is needed when the diagnosis remains uncertain after the clinical, neuropsychological and MRI assessment or when disease-modifying treatment is being considered [NIA_AA_2018] [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral parieto-occipital hypometabolism or hypoperfusion, right more than left, with relative sparing of frontal and medial temporal cortex
action_criteria.label: Consider FDG-PET, or perfusion SPECT where FDG-PET is not available, if the syndrome or its cause remains uncertain
action_criteria.rationale: A parieto-occipital functional pattern supports posterior cortical atrophy and separates it from corticobasal and Lewy body patterns; SPECT is the less accurate substitute [Foster_2007].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Fluoxetine (strong CYP2D6 inhibitor) can raise donepezil exposure: start low and monitor, or choose rivastigmine; no interaction with levetiracetam; labelled seizure warning in epilepsy
action_criteria.label: Check donepezil against fluoxetine and levetiracetam before starting a cholinesterase inhibitor
action_criteria.rationale: She takes fluoxetine, which inhibits donepezil metabolism, and has epilepsy, so the choice and titration of a cholinesterase inhibitor depend on this check [NICE_NG97].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the progressive visuospatial decline to her epilepsy, levetiracetam, depression or cataracts without completing the dementia work-up
Do not prescribe tramadol for her back pain or bupropion for her depression: both lower the seizure threshold, and tramadol with fluoxetine adds serotonin syndrome risk
Do not start memantine at the mild dementia stage; it is indicated for moderate or severe Alzheimer disease [NICE_NG97]
required_recommendations: Obtain collateral history from her husband about onset, course and daily function

Offer a trial of a cholinesterase inhibitor for mild Alzheimer dementia after checking pulse, conduction history and current medicines: with fluoxetine, start donepezil at 5 mg and titrate slowly, or choose rivastigmine; continue levetiracetam and ask her to report any seizure [NICE_NG97].

Offer amyloid biomarker testing (CSF or amyloid PET) if a biological diagnosis would change management, such as eligibility for anti-amyloid treatment or diagnostic uncertainty; one conclusive test is sufficient [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].
Refer to occupational therapy and low-vision services for visuospatial compensation, with a home assessment for the stairs after two falls [PCA_consensus_2017].
Address safety: confirm she no longer drives, review falls risk, medication handling and finances, and the support her husband can provide
Keep blood pressure at target and check lipids, given Fazekas grade 2 small vessel disease
Disclose the diagnosis and discuss prognosis, advance directives and a healthcare proxy with the patient and her husband

avoided_actions.rationale: Echocardiography is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication in this presentation
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; no arrhythmia, syncope, or palpitations described
MRI is available and not contraindicated; CT is less sensitive for the posterior atrophy pattern

accepted: Posterior cortical atrophy variant of early-onset Alzheimer's disease

differential.key_features: Raised by the maternal aunt's Lewy body dementia and the visual symptoms, but she has no hallucinations, parkinsonism, fluctuations or REM sleep behaviour disorder
Cortical sensory loss overlaps, but there is no limb apraxia, rigidity, dystonia, myoclonus or alien limb, and the involvement is bilateral parieto-occipital

differential.diagnosis: Cognitive impairment from focal epilepsy or antiseizure medication
differential.key_features: Seizure-free for over 3 years with a levetiracetam level in range; neither produces a progressive visuospatial syndrome with posterior cortical atrophy
Treated depression with a normal Geriatric Depression Scale (8/30); simultanagnosia and optic ataxia are not depressive features
Fazekas grade 2 white matter disease may contribute, but small vessel disease does not cause a posterior cortical syndrome with focal parieto-occipital atrophy
Gradual course; excluded by MRI showing atrophy without a lesion or restricted diffusion
Visual-onset CJD progresses over weeks with myoclonus; here the course is gradual over 18 months, there is no myoclonus, and MRI shows no restricted diffusion
Ophthalmology found stable acuity 20/25 with only mild cataracts; reading and scene-integration failure are higher-order visual deficits

key_clinical_evidence: In posterior cortical atrophy the presenting deficits are visuospatial and visuoperceptual with relatively preserved memory; patients often see an optometrist first, and Alzheimer pathology is the most common cause [PCA_consensus_2017].
Normal verbal memory, naming and fluency with marked visuospatial impairment is the PCA profile; a normal hippocampal volume does not argue against Alzheimer pathology in this variant
Family taking over driving after a collision and stopping work because of cognition mean instrumental independence is lost: the stage is mild dementia [NIA_AA_2011]
Fluoxetine inhibits CYP2D6 and raises donepezil exposure; rivastigmine, which is not CYP-metabolised, avoids the interaction [NICE_NG97]

findings.result: Alert; oriented to person, place, month and year but not the exact date.

MoCA 23/30: lost 2 visuospatial/executive points (incomplete clock, poorly reproduced cube), 1 on naming, 3 on delayed recall (2/5 free, 3/5 with category cues) and 1 on orientation (date). Serial 7s slow but accurate.

Cannot integrate the Cookie Theft scene (simultanagnosia); misreaches for a pen in the peripheral field (optic ataxia); difficulty shifting gaze between targets; reads aloud but cannot follow written paragraphs; slow detection in both lower quadrants on confrontation.

Husband: 18 months of progressive difficulty parking, finding objects in plain view and reading; disoriented driving in their neighbourhood of 30 years; two falls from misjudging stair edges. She recalls conversations, birthdays and the news.
Husband: more irritable and anxious in unfamiliar places; no personality change, disinhibition or hallucinations.

The family stopped her driving six months ago after a collision caused by misjudged distance; she retired because she could no longer plan lessons; her husband is concerned about her safety on the stairs.

Driving has been taken over by the family and she stopped work because of cognition, so instrumental independence is lost and the syndrome is at the mild dementia level.

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Elira Hoxha is a 66-year-old right-handed Albanian-American woman, a retired high school mathematics teacher, who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic for evaluation of progressive visuospatial difficulties and functional decline over approximately 18 months. Her husband first noticed changes roughly 18 months ago when she began having trouble parallel parking, a task she had always performed effortlessly. Around the same time, she started misplacing items not because she forgot where she put them, but because she seemed unable to visually locate objects sitting in plain view on the kitchen counter. Over the following months, she developed increasing difficulty reading, initially attributed to her known mild cataracts and hearing-related fatigue, but an ophthalmology evaluation confirmed stable visual acuity at 20/25 bilaterally with no explanation for her reading difficulties. She describes the text as appearing to 'jump around' and reports being unable to follow lines across a page. She has become reliant on audiobooks. Her husband reports that she has become disoriented while driving in their neighborhood of 30 years, missing turns and occasionally driving past their house. Six months ago, she had a minor fender-bender when she misjudged the distance to a parked car, and the family decided she should stop driving. She has also had two falls at home, both attributed to misjudging the position of stair edges. Importantly, her episodic memory has remained relatively intact — she accurately recalls conversations from days prior, remembers family birthdays, and follows current events through television news. Her husband notes she is emotionally more irritable and anxious than her baseline, particularly when navigating unfamiliar environments, but there have been no personality changes, no behavioral disinhibition, and no hallucinations. Her speech remains fluent and her word-finding is only mildly affected. The patient has a history of focal epilepsy diagnosed at age 58, which has been well-controlled on levetiracetam with no seizures in over 3 years. She also has a history of major depressive disorder treated with fluoxetine. Her neurologist referred her for further evaluation after noting the visuospatial complaints could not be explained by her seizure disorder or depression. There is concern about a neurodegenerative process given the progressive nature and functional impact, though the atypical presentation with preserved memory has made the referring physician uncertain about the diagnosis.

neurological_exam.additional: Simultanagnosia suggested by inability to describe the overall scene in the Boston Cookie Theft picture — identifies individual elements (woman, sink, cookies) but cannot integrate them into a coherent narrative. Optic ataxia suspected — misreaches when attempting to grab a pen held in peripheral visual field. Oculomotor apraxia not formally tested but patient exhibits difficulty shifting gaze smoothly between examiner's fingers in bilateral visual fields. No ideomotor apraxia. No limb-kinetic apraxia. No alien limb phenomenon.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin testing intact. Rapid alternating movements intact.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive to light, 3 mm bilaterally. Visual acuity 20/25 bilaterally with correction. Visual field testing by confrontation reveals subtle difficulty in bilateral lower quadrants — patient hesitant and slow to detect finger movements, though formal perimetry not performed. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. No ptosis. Facial sensation intact to light touch bilaterally. Facial movements symmetric. Hearing reduced bilaterally consistent with known sensorineural loss, improved with hearing aids. Palate elevates symmetrically. Shoulder shrug strong bilaterally. Tongue midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Gait steady with normal stride length and arm swing. Romberg negative. Tandem gait performed slowly but without falling. Patient occasionally misjudges doorway widths and bumps into doorframes during clinic visit.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person and place. Oriented to month and year but not exact date. Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score 23/30 with points lost on visuospatial/executive (clock drawing incomplete, cube copy poorly reproduced), naming (missed 1), and delayed recall (3/5 words recalled after cue). Able to spell WORLD backward. Language fluency grossly intact with occasional word-finding pauses. Able to follow 3-step commands. Reading aloud intact but reports difficulty comprehending written paragraphs. Serial 7s performed slowly but accurately.
neurological_exam.motor: Strength 5/5 throughout upper and lower extremities bilaterally. No pronator drift. Normal bulk and tone. No tremor at rest or with action.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+, triceps 2+, brachioradialis 2+, patellar 2+, Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffmann sign.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, temperature, vibration, and proprioception intact in all extremities. Graphesthesia impaired bilaterally in hands — unable to correctly identify numbers drawn on palms in 4 of 6 trials. Stereognosis mildly impaired in both hands — hesitant identification of common objects.
